newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik rebels release Austrian U.N. observer.
newsitem.headline: Tajik rebels release Austrian U.N. observer.

text.p: A rebel Tajik group holding several United Nations officials hostage on Tuesday released an Austrian military observer who was in poor health, a U.N. official said.
He said a U.N. military observer named as Major G. Hoenig had returned to the Tajik capital, Dushanbe.
he Tajik government said earlier on Tuesday it would bow to the demands of the rebel group holding the hostages by allowing the return of fellow rebels from Afghanistan to the ex-Soviet republic.

"At an urgent meeting held by (Tajik President Imomali) Rakhmonov in Dushanbe, the government has agreed to implement the fighters' demands," Rakhmonov's spokesman, Zafar Saidov, said by telephone. "Active negotiations are under way."
But he added that the method of exchange, and whether the 40 rebels in northern Afghanistan would be allowed to return with their weapons, had still to be decided.

Interfax news agency quoted field commander Bakhrom Sadirov, whose men have held hostages for eight days, as saying all the prisoners would be shot if the Tajik government failed to honour its commitment by 1500 GMT on Wednesday.
Sadirov accused Dushanbe of playing a "dirty political game" by encircling his forces and refusing to create a corridor of safe passage for his fellow rebels on the Afghan border.

Sadirov's brother, Tajik rebel leader Rizvon Sadirov, returned home from Afghanistan on Monday to help negotiate the release of the hostages. Rizvon Sadirov is now reported to be at his brother's base near the town of Obigarm in a mountainous area 80 km (50 miles) east of Dushanbe.

The hostage crisis began early last week when Bakhrom Sadirov's rebels seized four United Nations military observers. They later captured a carload of Russian reporters and four workers with the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR.
The crisis worsened on Saturday when the rebels seized Tajik Security Minister Saidamir Zukharov who had flown in to negotiate with the hostage-takers.
The hostage crisis comes just as the government and Islamist opposition rebels are trying to end a bitter four-year civil war that has left tens of thousands dead and many more homeless.
Saidov said the president had spoken to opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri on Tuesday and that both had agreed the kidnappings were "targeted against the process of reconciliation".
Rakhmonov and Nuri agreed on a ceasefire at a meeting in northern Afghanistan last December which appears to be holding.
Saidov said the two had agreed to hold a summit in the near future but gave no further details. A further round of peace talks is planned for February 26 in Moscow.

On Tuesday Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told a news briefing that Moscow was keen to help resolve the hostage crisis, which he said seriously hindered a broader solution of Tajikistan's problems.
